key_insight: Hardware-tailored pulses can replace gate sequences for modular VQE circuit elements, cutting quantum chemistry runtime substantially while preserving functionality.
engineering_relevance: This offers a scalable route to faster, more noise-resilient near-term quantum chemistry on hardware where long gate-based circuits are costly.
method: Use gradient-ascent pulse engineering to optimize pulses directly on the target quantum processor.
Implement modular VQE building blocks, especially single- and double-qubit excitations, as pulse-shaped circuit elements.
Assemble larger ansätze from these pulse-optimized primitives instead of optimizing a full circuit at once.
evidence_signal: On a silicon spin-qubit processor, the authors report excitation implementations in under 289 ns (single-qubit) and 927 ns (double-qubit), reducing VQE runtimes by up to 15.3× versus conventional gate-based methods.
watch_item: Full-ansatz pulse optimization becomes intractable as problem size grows, so practical deployment depends on reliable modular composition and hardware calibration.
paper_title: Pulse-optimised circuit elements for scalable and noise-resilient quantum chemistry
